strengths: Novel population-free partner generation framework with variance-based learnability-driven curriculum learning applied to partner-policy space; conceptually clear and well-motivated extension of dual curriculum design principles

Comprehensive experimental evaluation with strong empirical results: UPD achieves 94.4±8.1 average return on Overcooked-AI vs E3T's 76.8±9.7 and 58.9±5.9 on OGC vs SFL-E3T's 44.0±5.1; includes diverse evaluation populations, systematic ablations, and proper statistical testing

Human user study (12 participants, double-blind) demonstrates practical benefits beyond simulation: UPD rated significantly higher on adaptation (p<0.05), human-likeness (p<0.05), collaboration quality (p<0.05), and reduced frustration (p<0.05), addressing key evaluation gap in multi-agent coordination

Emerges beneficial behaviors without explicit design (e.g., convention-breaking in Figure 4) and seamlessly integrates with unsupervised environment design to enable joint curricula, directly addressing limitation identified by Ruhdorfer et al. (2025)

Strong reproducibility support through detailed hyperparameters (Tables 3-4), architecture specifications, infrastructure details, and promised code release; extensive appendix with training curves and learnability visualizations
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope: All evaluations confined to Overcooked-AI and OGC variants; no evidence of generalization to fundamentally different domains (Hanabi, football, etc.) despite claims of robust method; raises concern that insights may be domain-specific and limits real-world applicability

Narrow behavioral model captures only competence variability and action-level biases (Dirichlet sampling); explicitly missing strategic diversity, risk preferences, communication patterns; acknowledged limitation but not adequately justified that this subset suffices for 'robust' teamwork

Lacks theoretical foundation: No convergence guarantees, formal analysis of when/why variance-based selection maximizes learning, or principled justification for intermediate-difficulty prioritization; appears empirically motivated rather than grounded in curriculum learning theory

User study underpowered (only 12 participants, 3 layouts, narrow demographic range 26-34 years) with findings inconsistent with agent-only evaluation (e.g., MEP vs E3T ranking changes), suggesting evaluation modality matters significantly; calls into question generalizability of human results

OGC failure analysis incomplete: FC layout achieves only 17.1±4.2 return with minimal diagnosis; no systematic investigation of when variance-based selection fails; no runtime cost analysis despite 8,192×10 evaluations per iteration making computational overhead potentially high

Incremental algorithmic contribution: Core approach directly applies existing DCD framework to partner space; variance learnability adapted from Monette et al. (2025); mixture generation from E3T; limited novel algorithmic machinery or theoretical insights

Hyperparameter sensitivity underexplored: Claims 'one set of hyperparameters on all layouts' but involves grid search over buffer size, N, refresh frequency; Dirichlet parameter α=1.0 still requires tuning; no ablation of number of candidates (8,192) or sensitivity to buffer refresh frequency

Technical concerns: Coefficient-of-variation normalization (Eq. 5) numerically unstable for near-zero means; Figure 5 shows modest performance differences between learnability functions within error bars; limited justification for variance over robust alternatives (MAD, IQR)

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three environments (LBF, Overcooked-AI, OGC) with 282 trained policies and proper statistical reporting
Meaningful human-AI user study (12 participants) with appropriate controls, double-blind design, and statistical significance testing
Thorough ablations isolating components (bias, learnability) showing combined benefits; emergent convention-breaking behavior discovered and analyzed
Well-motivated problem framing: population-based AHT is expensive and E3T requires per-task tuning; UPD provides a clean population-free alternative
Natural extension to joint partner-environment curricula (JUPD) for procedurally generated environments, demonstrating framework generality
Detailed computational analysis (Appendix F) showing UPD is more efficient than population methods for reasonable parameters
Strong reproducibility support with extensive hyperparameters, algorithm clarity, and promised code release
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution directly applies variance-based learnability from Rutherford et al. (2024) and Monette et al. (2025) to partner selection with minimal algorithmic innovation

Critical issue with central claim: 'UPD w/o ℓ' achieves +14.1% vs E3T (only 4pp worse than full UPD at +18.0%), and Figure 19 shows all learnability functions perform similarly, suggesting benefits come from large-scale diverse sampling rather than learnability-driven selection

Improvements are modest and inconsistent across environments: substantial error bar overlap with baselines in several cases; UPD underperforms on CRoom (Table 1); weakest performance on FC layout dismissed without thorough investigation

Transparency concerns: Appendix B notes 'earlier version contained implementation and configuration issues affecting baseline experiments,' raising rigor concerns despite corrections; ROTATE comparison uses only 3 seeds vs. 6 for others

Hyperparameter tuning claims overclaimed: paper claims 'one set of hyperparameters for all layouts' but Table 5 shows fine-tuned UPD achieves +25.9% vs default +18.0%, contradicting central motivation

Limited scope and generalization: all experiments in simple grid-based discrete environments; OGC uses 5×5 version for tractability; no evaluation on continuous control or high-dimensional observation spaces

Learnability formulation underexplored: CV² normalization (Eq. 6) not justified; Figure 5 scatter plots very noisy; no analysis of buffer staleness as ego policy evolves; single threshold buffer management may not adapt well
Partner generator design (Alg. 2) relatively simple and ad-hoc; choice of Dirichlet-sampled biases not well justified; unclear how results generalize to different partner generators
Human study limitations: small sample (12 participants), only 3 of 5 layouts tested, generalization to diverse populations unclear

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three distinct environments (LBF, Overcooked-AI, OGC) with proper baselines (FCP, MEP, E3T, ROTATE) and ablations demonstrating each component's contribution
Principled theoretical grounding in Foster et al. (2026) connecting policy gradient variance to expected improvement, with learnability metric well-motivated for curriculum learning
Excellent reproducibility with extensive hyperparameter details (Tables 4-7), detailed appendices, transparency note about corrected implementation issues, and computational cost analysis
Strong human-AI validation study (n=12, double-blind, Holm-Bonferroni correction) showing UPD rated as more adaptive, human-like, and less frustrating than baselines
Practical efficiency demonstration: for vectorized simulators with n≥3 agents, UPD is cheaper than population-based methods while avoiding pre-training overhead
Interesting emergent phenomena including systematic convention-breaking dynamics (Figure 6) with analysis across multiple seeds and layouts
Clear, accessible presentation with good algorithmic descriptions and intuitive conceptual illustrations (Figure 2)
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: UPD is a relatively direct application of existing Sampling for Learnability (SFL; Rutherford et al., 2024) to partner policies rather than environments, representing incremental rather than fundamental innovation

Learnability scoring provides minimal value over random generation: UPD w/o ℓ achieves +14.1% vs E3T compared to full UPD's +18.0% (Table 1), suggesting most benefits come from large-scale online partner generation rather than the core learnability mechanism

Theory-practice gap not fully addressed: Foster et al. justifies advantage variance but UPD uses return variance; connection is plausible but not rigorously established for this setting, and CV² fix in JUPD suggests metric limitations

Modest performance improvements with frequent error bar overlap: In Table 1, UPD often underperforms or ties baselines on individual layouts (e.g., CRoom); UPD also underperforms relative to ROTATE on three layouts (Table 3)

Partner generator is simplistic and underexplored: Algorithm 2 uses only uniform ϵ sampling and Dirichlet action biases; limited to discrete actions, untested on continuous control, and choice to avoid richer partner spaces is under-justified for procedurally generated environments

Convention selection mechanism lacks rigorous justification (Section 4.4): causal claim that learnability causes convention-breaking via p=0.5 optimization is not established; alternative explanation is simply the randomness of partner generation itself

CV² normalization for JUPD appears ad-hoc: switching from ℓ_var to coefficient-of-variation squared to handle different reward scales is pragmatic but unprincipled; why CV² over other normalization schemes?

OGC experiments have limited scope: only 5×5 version tested, cannot compare to classical population-based methods, baselines all lack learnability filtering, and procedural environment setting feels somewhat disconnected from main contribution

Inconsistent experimental methodology: different seed counts across experiments (3 vs 6), self-play baseline appears under-tuned (-62% vs E3T), and limited hyperparameter search relative to carefully-tuned ROTATE comparison
Missing ablations on key hyperparameters: buffer refresh frequency R, sensitivity to buffer size beyond Table 7 search, and scalability to team sizes larger than 2 agents not explored
